name: Tualatin / Twalatin
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Hajda, Yvonne P. 1976. Mary's River Kalapuyan: A Descriptive Phonology. MA thesis, Portland State University (PDXScholar; doi:10.15760/etd.2488), p.45 'Suprasegmentals'; Lewis, J. William. 2003. Central Kalapuya phonology: the segmental inventory of John Hudson's Santiam. MA thesis, University of Victoria, p.116 fn.50 and p.210 with fn.101. Both are descriptions of Central Kalapuya varieties whose Tualatin statements are comparative asides drawn from Frachtenberg/Jacobs manuscripts and Berman's Louis Kenoyer slip files. Corroborated by Hajda, Yvonne 1976. The Phonemes of Mary's River Kalapuyan: Analyzing an Extinct Language. Papers for the 11th International Conference on Salish Languages (UBC lingpapers), 13 pp., p.10 section 'Stress' (same Tualatin/Yoncalla statement, published version).
catalog_locator: Hajda 1976 thesis p.45 (section 'Suprasegmentals'); Lewis 2003 p.116 with fn.50 and examples (43)-(44) (Ch.3 Resonants, sec.3.5.2 'Geminates in Northern Kalapuya compared with CK') and p.210 with fn.101 (Ch.5 Occlusives); Hajda 1976 ICSNL p.10 (section 'Stress')
catalog_quote: Hajda 1976:45: "It occurs on both short and long vowels, and is thus independent of length ... In Mary's River, it falls on the first syllable of a stem; in Tualatin and Yoncalla, stress is often shifted to prefixed elements. If a prefix is added in Mary's River, stress does not move: waú·tso?, kuwaú·tso?. Stress is accompanied generally by higher pitch (sometimes perhaps by lower pitch), which Jacobs calls "pitch accent." He says that pitch accent falls on "every syllable felt to be an independent root--nominal, pronominal, connective, or verbal" (1930: n.p.). Since stress is not always predictable from the segmental construction alone, it is considered to be phonemic." Lewis 2003:116 fn.50: "Stress is more complex in Twalatin; monosyllabic short roots take stress on the penultimate (where, if having variable vowels, roots may be long anyway)." Lewis 2003:210: "in unsuffixed roots in Twalatin, for example, the accent has regressed into the prefix system.[101]" fn.101: "This follows a penultimate stress pattern of Columbia River languages." Hajda 1976 ICSNL:10: "Stress is independent of length. It falls on the first syllable of a root in Mary's River and Santiam, remaining there when prefixes are added, although in Tualatin and Yoncalla it is often shifted to the prefixed elements."
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kalapuyan generally has a (pitch-)accent on the first syllable of the root/stem (so described first-hand for Mary's River and Santiam Central Kalapuya). For Tualatin (Northern Kalapuya) the only accessible statements are incidental comparative remarks in these Central-Kalapuya theses: stress is 'often shifted to prefixed elements' (Hajda), i.e. with a short monosyllabic root the stress lands on the preceding (prefix) syllable = the penult of the word (Lewis). No full rule for Tualatin is given; the system looks root-based with weight-conditioned retraction, but this is not worked out in any source I could open.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing for Tualatin. (Lewis 2003:63 fn.14, for Central Kalapuya: secondary stress on the left-most syllabic nucleus of pronominals/adverbials.)
new_statements.exceptions: Lewis: monosyllabic short roots take penultimate (prefix) stress; roots with 'variable vowels' may be long anyway. Hajda: shift to prefixes is 'often', not always.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress/pitch accent as marked in Frachtenberg's and Jacobs' text transcriptions (connected texts, not citation forms); Hajda treats stress as phonemic and accompanied by higher pitch (Jacobs' 'pitch accent'). Both remarks about Tualatin are made in passing in descriptions of Central Kalapuya varieties (Mary's River; Santiam), based on Frachtenberg/Jacobs manuscripts and Berman's Tualatin slip files from Louis Kenoyer.
new_statements.identity_note: Both quoted remarks concern the Tualatin (Tfalati/Atfalati, 'Twalatin') dialect of Northern Kalapuya as recorded from Louis Kenoyer and earlier Gatschet/Frachtenberg consultants; nothing was found on the Yamhill dialect. The host works describe Central Kalapuya varieties (Mary's River and Santiam, glottocode kala1402 'Kalapuya' / Central Kalapuya [kyl]); their Tualatin statements are comparative asides, not a description of tual1242 in its own right. Hajda groups Tualatin with Yoncalla (Southern Kalapuya, sout2964) as both showing stress shift onto prefixes.

new_statements.relation_note: Consistent with the catalog record (Hajda 1976:45, which itself relays Jacobs): stress independent of vowel length and 'accompanied generally by higher pitch.. which Jacobs calls pitch accent' = Jacobs 1945 pp.15, 152 'stress accent.. always one with slightly higher pitch'. Jacobs 1945 is SILENT on placement: it neither confirms nor contradicts Hajda's 'first syllable of a stem; in Tualatin and Yoncalla stress is often shifted to prefixed elements' or Lewis 2003's root-initial pitch accent (those come from Jacobs's unpublished c.1930 grammatical sketch, Box 70.2, not from this volume). The catalog's hedged/unclear status for Tualatin therefore stands; the p.153 remark that Tualatin geminati…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Jacobs describes the NATURE of Kalapuya (incl. Tualatin) word stress, not its POSITION: a weak but definite stress accent that always coincides with slightly higher pitch (a tonal step of at most a second or third above the word's base tone; in Santiam, level high tone on long syllables); Tualatin shares the Santiam phoneme system except that it lacks the Santiam incomplete final-consonant articulation with glottal closure, and it has consonant gemination/lengthening 'determined by syllable weighting' (non-phonemic). No rule for which syllable carries the stress is stated anywhere in the phonetic keys or prefaces; stress is instead marked word by word with an accent mark after the stressed vowel throughout the texts (Tualatin texts pp.155-198, Yamhill/Tualatin pp.199-203), so the volume is primary data for a placement study but makes no placement claim. Jacobs defers Tualatin phonetics proper to 'the monograph to follow' (p.86) and notes (pp.146-147) that Gatschet and Frachtenberg wrote proclitics, enclitics and sometimes prefixes as separate words and that Frachtenberg over-marked vowel length, which bears on reading accent marks in the older Tualatin texts.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress. Related prosodic detail only: pitch rise co-occurs with stress; Santiam long stressed syllables carry level high tone (p.15); Tualatin consonant lengthening varies by 'syllable weighting' (p.153).
new_statements.exceptions: None as to stress placement (no placement rule given). Dialect differences noted: Tualatin lacks the Santiam CV'C weak glottal closure of light syllables (p.86); Tualatin has vowel e, e· and variant ei (p.152) and characteristic geminated consonants (p.153).
new_statements.identity_note: Jacobs 1945 Part III 'Phonetics' (pp.151-153) is a key for all Kalapuya dialects printed in the volume, with Tualatin-specific remarks (vowel e, gemination); the Tualatin (= Atfalati, 'Tualatin or Wappato Lake dialect', Northern Kalapuya) material is Gatschet's 1877 Grand Ronde texts from Peter Kinai, Yatchkawa and others, partly rechecked with the last speaker Louis Kenoyer (b. c.1867, d. 1937) by Frachtenberg 1914 and Jacobs 1936, plus Kenoyer's 1936 word-for-word Tualatin translations of five Santiam myths (pp.135-142) and of Louisa Selky's 1914 Yamhill myth (pp.199-203). Part I p.15 describes Santiam (Central Kalapuya, kala1400), which p.86 says Tualatin matches 'almost entirely' except for the absence of the Santiam light-syllable final glottal closure.
